description: We are a team of CSE students and tech enthusiasts interested in AI, computer vision, remote sensing, and building practical solutions with real-world data. We enjoy turning complex datasets into useful, interactive applications and are especially interested in Earth observation and space technology.For this challenge, we are exploring NISAR-based surface change detection and visualization.
summary:
AccessWatch is an offline mobile app that shows relief teams which communities a flood has cut off from help, and how to reach them.

We built a pipeline that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar data into answers. Radar sees through clouds, rain and darkness, so it works in exactly the weather a flood brings. By comparing scenes from before and after the flood, we map the new water, refined by a machine-learning model checked against the official Copernicus emergency map (IoU 0.82 in spatial cross-validation, against 0.68 for a simple threshold). We estimate water depth from a terrain model, mark every road as passable or not by car, high-clearance vehicle or on foot, and combine this with population and service data to find areas cut off from clinics, food and shelter.

On a real flood from January 2026, AccessWatch found 8 cut-off areas with about 13,100 people. The app ranks them, tells teams whether to bring a boat or a truck, shows the safest route, and shares ready-to-send alerts.

It matters because the people hardest to see after a flood are often the ones who need help most.
details:
What it does and how it works

AccessWatch finds the communities a flood has cut off from help, and shows relief teams how to reach them.

1. Flood map: we compare NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar scenes from before and after a flood. Radar sees through clouds, rain and darkness, so it works in the weather a flood brings. Automatic thresholds give a first flood map, which a machine-learning model (gradient boosting) refines using the official Copernicus emergency flood map as labels. In spatial cross-validation it reached an IoU of 0.82, against 0.68 for the threshold map alone.

2. Water depth: estimated from the flood edges and a 30 m terrain model, shown as shallow, medium or deep.

3. Roads: every OpenStreetMap road piece is marked as passable or not for a car, a high-clearance vehicle and on foot. Bridges the radar cannot assess are flagged.

4. Cut-off areas: combining roads, clinics, markets, shelters and WorldPop population, we find areas that lost access to services, rank them by people affected, services lost and difficulty, and plan the safest and shortest routes, including boat crossings.

5. Mobile app: the results are checked and packed into an offline Flutter app. It has a flood map with one-tap layer buttons and a full-screen view, a "Who needs help" list, area pages with water depth and lost services, safest routes, ready-to-send team alerts in English and Portuguese, a nearest-clinic finder, and a short first-run tour.

On a real flood from January 2026, AccessWatch found 8 cut-off areas with about 13,100 people.

Benefits

Relief teams learn where cut-off people are, how many there are, what to bring (a boat or a high-clearance vehicle) and which way is safest, without waiting for clear skies or ground reports. The app works without internet, which is common in flood areas.

Intended impact

Faster, better-targeted help for the people hardest to see after a flood. Our goal is for teams to get these answers within hours of a disaster, for any flood NISAR observes, so that no community is forgotten because its road disappeared.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python on Kaggle Notebooks: NumPy, GeoPandas, Rasterio, Shapely, NetworkX, OSMnx, asf_search and scikit-learn.

Dart and Flutter for the app: flutter_map, Riverpod and go_router, with automated tests and an Android release build.

Data: NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV, Copernicus Emergency Management Service, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, JRC Global Surface Water, OpenStreetMap and WorldPop.

Hardware: laptops and an Android phone for testing.

AI assistance: Claude helped write code, review results and prepare documents; all results were run and checked by our team.

How it is creative

Most flood tools stop at "where is the water". AccessWatch asks "who can no longer reach help", by turning a radar flood map into a road network problem. Every road is checked for each type of vehicle, and each cut-off area becomes a clear task card that says what to bring and which way to go.

Factors our team considered

Honesty: the app shows that NISAR data is first-release, that depth and population are estimates, and what to check on the ground.

Validation: the flood map is tested on areas the model never saw.

Offline use and low-end phones: everything works without internet.

Accessibility: large text up to 200%, big touch targets, screen-reader labels, and English and Portuguese.

Privacy: location stays on the phone.

Safety: AccessWatch supports decisions; it is not an emergency service.

Open source: the code is public so others can test and improve it.
